name: Hassaniya Arabic (Mauritanian)
notes: Ḥassāniyya Arabic (klām əl-Bīđ̣ān), the Bedouin Maghrebi dialect of Mauritania, Western Sahara and the borderlands of Mali/Algeria/southern Morocco, described by Taine-Cheikh (2007, EALL 'Ḥassāniyya Arabic', pp.240-250) and Cohen (1963). It is a conservative Bedouin dialect that is typologically closer to eastern Arabic than to sedentary Maghrebi. DEFINING FEATURES: (1) qāf ق → [ɡ] (Taine-Cheikh §2.1.1.2 'the realization of qāf as [g]'); [q] survives in Classical borrowings and, for most speakers, as the merger reflex of ġayn — /ġ/ and /q/ merge to [q] outside the west, and always under gemination (§2.1.1.1). (2) THE INTERDENTALS ARE RETAINED: ث [θ], ذ [ð], and ḍād ض → đ̣ [ðˤ] 'the reflex of most words with ḍād' (§2.1.1.2), merging with ẓāʾ ظ [ðˤ]. (3) THE ḤASSĀNIYYA /v/: the labial spirant *f is realised PREFERENTIALLY AS VOICED [v] — 'except in contact with a voiceless consonant or when it is geminate' (§2.1.1.3); that voiceless-context devoicing back to [f] is conditioned by an adjacent consonant and is not expressed as a rule here (the transcription keeps [v] there — a documented under-generation). LOAN EXEMPTION: Taine-Cheikh scopes the labial-spirant voicing to the INHERITED *f only, so recent European loans keep [f] and do not voice — التِّلِيفُون 'the telephone' (< French téléphone) → [ttilifuːn], not *[ttilivuːn] (arbitrated gold, both judges). Because the ف→[v] map is a grapheme candidate that cannot distinguish an inherited *f from a loan /f/, the loan is carried as a word_exceptions entry. This voiced reflex, written ⟨ڤ⟩, is 'particular to this dialect' and is its most famous consonantal trait (dvəl 'to spit', šāvu 'they saw'). (4) ǧīm ج → [ʒ] (§2.1.1.3 '/j/ is realized as a palato-alveolar fricative'). (5) RICH EMPHATIC SYSTEM: Ḥassāniyya phonemicises emphasis widely — /ṛ/ [rˤ] (more frequent than plain /r/), /ḷ/ [lˤ], and /ẓ/ [zˤ] borrowed from Zenaga Berber, alongside /tˤ dˤ sˤ ðˤ/ and marginal velarised /ḅ ṃ ṇ ṿ/ — with minimal pairs like walla 'to come back' vs waḷḷa 'or', dār 'to put' vs dāṛ 'to want' (§2.1.1.1). These emphatic sonorants are lexical, not predictable from the abjad, so they are documented here but emitted only through the inherited emphasis backing of /a aː/ → [ɑ ɑː]. VOWELS (§2.1.2): long /iː uː aː/, short /a ə/, with /i/ and /u/ merged to /ə/ in closed syllables (a nomadic trait, Cohen 1970); /a/ undergoes ʔimāla to a centralized [æ] (žä 'he came'). DIPHTHONGS (§2.1.3): the four Classical diphthongs /aj aw ij uw/ are PRESERVED, with /aj aw/ variably tending to [eː oː]. Berber (Zenaga) substrate and Black-African (Wolof/Fula/Soninke) contact add marginal phonemes (palatalised /dy ty ny/, /ŋ/). LOAN GRAPHEME ݣ. Two facts, each cited, and the load-bearing one is this spec own. What the letter is: U+0763 ARABIC LETTER KEHEH WITH THREE DOTS ABOVE, the form-B kaf with three dots whose function is to write /ɡ/ — Kew 2003 (Unicode L2/03-176) section 3 states that pairing for Morocco with photographic evidence. That Hassaniyya has the sound: /ɡ/ is this spec own qaf reflex, read first, on Taine-Cheikh 2007 pp.240-250 and Watson 2002 *q → [ɡ] in Bedouin dialects. CORROBORATION RATHER THAN LICENCE: Kew p.6 Figure 12 (from Norris 1968 p.73) notes that a similar form is seen in Mauritanian texts, where a kaf written in shape B with three dots added is also used to represent /ɡ/. A figure extending a form to Mauritanian text is weaker than the section 3 sentence it extends, which is stated for Morocco, so it corroborates and does not carry the key on its own. THE CORPUS IS SILENT HERE, not contradicting: lahgtna thirteen dialect labels include no Mauritanian one, so no count either supports or opposes this reading.

sources.notes: Read (open-access HAL author manuscript). §2.1: qāf → [g] and interdental retention (§2.1.1.2); labial spirant → voiced [v] except before/after a voiceless consonant or when geminate (§2.1.1.3); ǧīm → [ʒ]; the emphatic system incl. /ṛ ḷ ẓ/ with minimal pairs (§2.1.1.1); vowels /iː uː aː/ + /a ə/, i/u merger in closed syllables, ʔimāla (§2.1.2); the four diphthongs preserved (§2.1.3).

sources.author: Kew, J. (SIL International)
sources.title: Proposal to encode Jawi and Moroccan Arabic GAF characters
sources.notes: The encoding proposal behind U+0763, and the only source that states the letter-to-sound pairing outright — the Moroccan grammars transcribe in Latin and so never name a letter. §3: 'Although standard Arabic does not write a /ɡ/ sound, in Morocco the use of a form B kaf with three dots above is well established as the letter representing /ɡ/.' Evidence is photographic — a street name, a petrol pump labelled 'gasoil', a 'Megamag' medicine package, and the Royal Moroccan Academy's Amazigh dictionary (Shafiq 1996 p.136). p.6 extends it: 'A similar form is seen in Mauritanian texts, where a kaf written in shape B with three dots added is also used to represent /ɡ/' (Figure 12, from Norris 1968 p.73). TRAPS: the proposal notes the letter is visually identical to U+06AD ARABIC LETTER NG in initial and medial joined forms, so the two are confusable in real text and both occur; and it states that published literature is in standard Arabic and does not use the letter, so frequency in edited prose tests nothing about its status.

sources.author: The Unicode Consortium
sources.title: The Unicode Standard, code chart: Arabic (Range 0600-06FF)
sources.notes: Read (chart PDF and the matching NamesList.txt). U+06A2 is named ARABIC LETTER FEH WITH DOT MOVED BELOW and annotated 'Maghrib Arabic'; U+0763 is ARABIC LETTER KEHEH WITH THREE DOTS ABOVE, annotated 'Moroccan Arabic, Amazigh, Burushaski'. The names are normative. Cited for the identity of the letters and for nothing about their phonetic value, which each entry sources separately.

stress.notes: Arabic stress is QUANTITY-SENSITIVE: it falls on a syllable because that syllable is heavy, not because of any orthographic ending, so no ending table can express it. The cascade (Ryding, A Reference Grammar of MSA, CUP 2005, §2.3; Watson, The Phonology and Morphology of Arabic, OUP 2002, ch.3): a superheavy final syllable (CVːC/CVCC) takes the stress (kiˈtaːb); otherwise a heavy penult (CVː/CVC) does (muˈdarris); otherwise the antepenult (ˈmadrasa). max_onset=1 because Arabic onsets are obligatory and hold exactly one consonant — a medial cluster splits, closing the preceding syllable, and that boundary is what makes the penult of mudarris heavy. INPUT CONTRACT: weight is only recoverable from a complete transcription, so this requires diacritized input; an undiacritized skeleton has no vowels to weigh. The registered wikipron gold carries no stress marks, but the benchmark strips stress from both sides by default, so this costs no PER. Prosodic clitics: monosyllabic function words (negator maː, prepositions fiː/min/ʕan/ʕa/li/bi, vocative jaː, copula-negator muː/miʃ, conditional law/loː, wa-proclitic combinations) attach to a host and fall inside the host's stress domain, so they carry no word stress (Watson 2002, The Phonology and Morphology of Arabic, OUP, ch.3). Pan-Arabic class; the per-lect form list reflects the function words attested in this lect. Orthographic test — a clitic homograph (e.g. verb yā 'came') is destressed in every occurrence.
